title: Anaphylaxis (food-triggered)

card.complaint: Lip swelling, rash and breathlessness 15 minutes after lunch

triage.note: Arrived by taxi with a friend. Ate a cashew curry at a restaurant 15 minutes ago. Itchy rash, swollen lips, “throat feels tight”, wheezy and lightheaded.

ivAdrenalineHarm: Never give 1 mg of 1 mg/mL adrenaline as an IV bolus to a patient with a pulse: it can cause severe hypertension, VT/VF and myocardial ischaemia. In anaphylaxis IV adrenaline is given only as a titrated infusion by experienced staff.

speech.impairedText: (Hoarse and gasping. He can only nod or shake his head.)

appearance.text: Settled. Talking in full sentences. Hives fading.
Anxious but improving. Voice clearer, a little wheeze.
Flushed with widespread hives and swollen lips. Audible wheeze, speaking in short phrases.
Pale and clammy. Hoarse voice, stridor, getting drowsy.

history.a: I was eating lunch… a cashew curry. About 15 minutes later my lips started tingling, then this rash, and now my throat feels tight. I feel dizzy.
I’m allergic to peanuts. I had hives once as a kid. I didn’t know cashews could do this.

history.q: Do you carry an adrenaline auto-injector?
history.a: I was given one years ago. It expired and I stopped carrying it.

history.q: Is your breathing or swallowing affected?
history.a: My throat’s tight and it’s hard to swallow. My chest feels wheezy.
Mild asthma. I use a blue inhaler maybe once a month.
Just the salbutamol inhaler. Nothing else.

history.q: Any vomiting, tummy pain or fainting?
history.a: I feel sick and crampy. I nearly fainted walking in.

history.q: Any alcohol, exercise or smoking today?
history.a: I had one beer with lunch. I don’t smoke.

history.q: Ask the friend what they saw
history.a: His lips swelled up really fast and he kept coughing. In the taxi he looked like he was going to pass out.

exam.label: Airway
exam.text: Lips and tongue swollen. Hoarse voice, soft inspiratory stridor. Managing secretions.

variants.text: Lip swelling reducing. No stridor. Voice normal.
Marked tongue swelling, loud stridor, pooling secretions. The airway is at risk.

exam.label: Breathing
exam.text: Widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry at the bases. Using accessory muscles.

variants.text: Occasional wheeze only. Good air entry bilaterally.

exam.label: Circulation
exam.text: Weak, rapid radial pulse. Capillary refill 4 s. Cool peripheries.

variants.text: Warm peripheries, capillary refill under 2 s, good-volume pulse.

exam.label: Disability
exam.text: GCS 15, anxious. Pupils equal and reactive.

exam.label: Exposure / skin
exam.text: Widespread raised urticarial wheals on the trunk and arms, facial flushing. No sting marks.

exam.label: Abdomen
exam.text: Soft, mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding.

investigations.label: Venous blood gas
investigations.text: pH 7.31, pCO₂ 44 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, K⁺ 3.9 mmol/L.

variants.text: pH 7.38, pCO₂ 40 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 23 mmol/L, lactate 1.9 mmol/L, K⁺ 3.8 mmol/L.

investigations.label: 12-lead ECG
investigations.text: Sinus tachycardia. Normal axis. No ST changes.

investigations.label: Mast cell tryptase (timed)
investigations.text: Sample taken and labelled with the time. Result in 24–48 h. Repeat at 1–2 h and at ≥ 24 h or at allergy follow-up.

investigations.label: Urea & electrolytes
investigations.text: Na⁺ 139, K⁺ 3.9 mmol/L, creatinine 84 µmol/L (0.95 mg/dL).

investigations.label: Chest X-ray (portable)
investigations.text: Mild hyperinflation. No consolidation, no pneumothorax.

interventions.label: Call for help
interventions.say: Nurse: “Resus team called. The senior is on the way.”

interventions.label: Lie flat, legs raised
interventions.detail: Sit up only if breathing is worse lying flat
interventions.say: Nurse: “Laid flat with his legs up.”

interventions.label: Salbutamol 5 mg nebulised
interventions.feedback: Bronchodilators help persisting wheeze but do not replace IM adrenaline.

interventions.label: Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM
interventions.detail: 0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL (1:1000), anterolateral thigh. Repeat after 5 min if no better
interventions.say: Nurse: “Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM given into the thigh.”

interventions.label: Adrenaline IV infusion
interventions.detail: Refractory anaphylaxis only; senior / critical-care led
interventions.feedback: Appropriate for refractory anaphylaxis (ABC problems persisting after two doses of IM adrenaline), with critical-care support and continuous monitoring.

interventions.label: Crystalloid 500 mL IV bolus
interventions.detail: Hartmann’s or 0.9% saline, rapid; repeat as needed

interventions.label: Chlorphenamine 10 mg IV
interventions.feedback: Antihistamines treat skin features only. They do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems and are not part of initial resuscitation (RCUK 2021). A non-sedating oral antihistamine is preferred once stable.

interventions.label: Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV
interventions.feedback: Routine corticosteroids are no longer advised in the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (RCUK 2021). Consider them only after initial resuscitation, e.g. for refractory reactions or ongoing asthma or shock.

dispositions.label: Discharge home now with oral antihistamines
Observe (≥ 6–12 h); discharge with 2 adrenaline auto-injectors, training, written plan and allergy referral
Admit to general ward for IV steroids

critical.label: IM adrenaline given
critical.why: IM adrenaline is the first-line treatment. Give it as soon as anaphylaxis is recognised; delay is associated with death.

critical.label: High-flow oxygen
critical.why: Hypoxaemia with airway and breathing compromise.

critical.label: IV fluid bolus for hypotension
critical.why: Anaphylactic shock is distributive; large volumes of crystalloid may be needed.

critical.label: Monitoring attached
critical.why: Continuous ECG, SpO₂ and BP are needed to judge the response to treatment.

recommended.label: Identified asthma (risk factor for severe reactions)
Sent a timed mast cell tryptase

teaching: Anaphylaxis: sudden Airway and/or Breathing and/or Circulation problems, usually with skin or mucosal changes, after exposure to a trigger. Skin features can be absent.
Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (adult) into the anterolateral thigh is first-line. Repeat after 5 minutes if there is no improvement. Do not wait for IV access.
ABC problems persisting after two IM doses = refractory anaphylaxis: get critical-care help and start a low-dose IV adrenaline infusion with continuous monitoring.
Never give 1 mg of undiluted adrenaline IV to a patient with a pulse.
Antihistamines and corticosteroids are not first-line and do not treat ABC problems.
Give 500–1000 mL crystalloid boluses (adult) for hypotension and repeat as needed.
Tryptase: take a sample as soon as resuscitation allows, again at 1–2 h, and a baseline at ≥ 24 h.
Before discharge: observation period according to response, two adrenaline auto-injectors with training, a written plan and referral to an allergy clinic.
references: Resuscitation Council UK. Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis: guidelines for healthcare providers (2021).
